quote: Deciding how to treat a burn depends first on assessing its depth, which separates injuries that heal with conservative care from those that need surgery \citep{jackson}. Burns are graded as first degree (epidermis only), second degree (partial thickness, into the dermis), or third degree (full thickness) \citep{heimbach}.
location: Section 1 (Introduction), manuscript.tex line 112; and Section 3.6 line 235 (BIP_US mapping); Section 4.6 line 462
problem: The two sentences are clinically incompatible, and the paper never notices. The conservative-versus-surgical boundary is NOT first/second/third: it lies between superficial partial-thickness (papillary dermis; blanches, heals in under ~3 weeks with dressings) and deep partial-thickness / deep dermal (reticular dermis; sluggish or absent blanching, reduced pinprick sensation; will not heal in 3 weeks and is generally excised and grafted). Both are 'second degree'. So the model's three-class output cannot express the decision the Introduction says depth assessment exists to make. Heimbach 1984, the cited authority, is itself a study of predicting healing within 3 weeks, not a defence of a three-tier degree scale. The BIP_US section is the direct symptom: 'because the mapping onto our three classes is not exact, we report both plausible mappings of deep dermal (to second degree and to third degree)'. Deep dermal is anatomically partial thickness, i.e. second degree; mapping it to third degree is a MANAGEMENT equivalence, not a depth equivalence, and the paper calls both 'plausible' without saying which kind of equivalence each is. The mapping ambiguity exists only because the label space collapses the one distinction that drives treatment. Words 'surgery', 'surgical', 'graft' and 'excis' appear nowhere else in the 812-line manuscript; 'superficial dermal' and 'deep dermal' appear only in that one mapping sentence.
why_it_matters: Major revision. A burn-surgeon referee will say the Introduction motivates a clinical task the system's label space cannot perform, and that a paper whose external-validation section turns on a deep-dermal mapping must state the anatomy/management distinction explicitly. Required: rewrite the depth taxonomy to name superficial partial vs deep partial, state that the surgical decision boundary falls inside the 'second degree' class, justify each BIP_US mapping on its own grounds, and report the under-grading count under both mappings (the manuscript reports only one).
evidence: Recomputed from /Volumes/RayTOSHIBA/مشروع تخرج ١/01_paper/statistics/external_validation_BIPUS.json (94 rows; Table 6 confusion matrix reproduces exactly: SD 13/27/2, DD 25/7/0, FT 10/7/3). Under deep-dermal→second, 55 of 94 are under-graded and third-degree recall is 3/20 = 15.0%. Under deep-dermal→third, 62 of 94 are under-graded and third-degree recall is 3/52 = 5.8%. The manuscript states 'about 55 of 94 images below their true severity' (line 462) and repeats it in the Table 6 caption without naming the mapping; the figure is mapping-dependent and the alternative is 62. The results JSON itself records only one: "note": "...deep dermal mapped to Second".

quote: the shipped demonstration application runs a Swin-Small classifier rather than the benchmarked Swin-Tiny, so no number in this paper describes what a user of the application experiences.
location: Section 4.11 (Efficiency), manuscript.tex line 675; cf. Section 3.3 line 198, Ethics line 787, Data Availability line 793
problem: The configuration that a person can actually run — and whose weights the authors publicly release — is the one configuration the paper never evaluated. The paper concedes this twice ('The mobile demonstration currently ships a Swin-Small classifier, whereas all pipeline numbers reported in this paper use the benchmarked Swin-Tiny weights', line 198), yet the Data Availability statement ships it anyway: weights are 'attached to the tagged release there: ... and the classifier shipped in the mobile demonstration'. Meanwhile the single explicit safety statement — 'it must not be used for clinical decision-making' — appears exactly once, at line 787, inside the Ethics declaration at the very end of the paper. It is absent from the abstract, absent from the Conclusion, and it will not travel with a downloaded weight file. This is a burn-severity grader that the paper itself shows under-grades 28.3 percent of eligible external images and assigns first degree to 10 of 20 full-thickness burns.
why_it_matters: Major revision, and an editor may hold the paper on it. A tool that systematically errs toward lower severity is exactly the tool whose disclaimer must be unmissable. Required: put the non-clinical-use statement in the abstract and the Conclusion, not only in the Ethics block; either benchmark the shipped Swin-Small configuration on both test sets or withdraw it from the release; and attach a prominent warning plus a use restriction to the repository README and the tagged release, so the caveat is co-located with the artifact rather than with the paper.
evidence: grep over manuscript.tex: the string 'must not be used' occurs at line 787 only; 'not a clinically validated device' occurs only at lines 198 and 203 (Section 3.3 body and the Figure 1 caption). The abstract (lines 96-102) and Conclusion (lines 771-777) contain neither string. Under-grading rates are the paper's own: '28.3 percent externally (51 of 180)' (line 464); Table 6 gives full-thickness predicted first = 10 of 20, confirmed against external_validation_BIPUS.json.

quote: The right reading is therefore not that the model cannot rank burn depth, but that it applies a severity scale systematically offset from clinical depth staging, and offset in the dangerous direction.
location: Section 4.6 (External validation), manuscript.tex line 464
problem: This is the one place in an otherwise unusually candid paper where the authors let themselves off. The rescuing statistic — 'Restricting the comparison to the 46 images on which the model does commit to a class the reference can contain, balanced accuracy rises to 62.2 and 55.4 percent' — conditions the denominator on the model's own output. That is selection on the outcome: the 62.2 percent is not an estimate of performance on any pre-specifiable population of patients, and it cannot support a positive claim about depth ranking. Within that hand-picked subset the entire claim rests on 3 of 10 committed full-thickness burns being called third degree. Clinically the raw matrix reads the other way: 0 of 32 deep dermal burns were called third degree and 25 of 32 were called first degree; 17 of 20 full-thickness burns were graded below third. 'Offset' also implies a correctable calibration shift — that re-mapping or re-thresholding could rescue the model — which is a materially more optimistic conclusion than the data license, and it sits oddly beside the paper's own 'the model does not generalise to clinical data' two sentences later.
why_it_matters: Major revision. A referee will ask the authors to delete the 'not that the model cannot rank burn depth' inference or restate it as explicitly exploratory, to flag the 62.2/55.4 figures as conditioned on the model's own predictions and therefore not performance estimates, and to report the third-degree recall on the full set (15.0% or 5.8% depending on mapping) alongside them. The correction strengthens the paper: it makes the external failure cleaner, which is the direction the paper's own thesis wants.
evidence: Recomputed from external_validation_BIPUS.json. Deep-dermal→second: third-degree recall 3/20 = 15.0%; second-degree recall 34/74 = 45.9%; balanced 30.5% (matches the manuscript). Deep-dermal→third: third-degree recall 3/52 = 5.8%; second-degree recall 27/42 = 64.3%; balanced 35.0% (matches). The 46-image subset is 94 minus the 48 first-degree calls, i.e. defined entirely by the model's predictions.

quote: Class shares are approximately 42 percent first degree, 31 percent second, and 27 percent third. The labels are community-provided and were not independently verified by clinicians.
location: Section 3.1 (Dataset), manuscript.tex line 154; cf. Section 5.3 line 717
problem: A 42 percent first-degree share is not a plausible clinical distribution and is a stronger, more specific diagnosis of the BIP_US collapse than the one the paper offers. First-degree burns are epidermal erythema; they are excluded from TBSA estimation, are not referred for depth assessment, and do not appear in clinical burn photography — which is exactly why BIP_US, a real clinical database, contains none. The paper's largest training class is therefore a category that is close to vestigial in the target clinical setting, and that prior is the direct mechanism by which the pipeline dumps 48 of 94 clinical images (51 percent) into a class 'that cannot be correct under either mapping'. The Discussion instead attributes the collapse vaguely to 'a narrow, web-sourced training distribution and a labelling protocol that differs from clinical depth staging' (line 717), which states the symptom without naming the cause the authors' own Table 1 puts in front of them.
why_it_matters: Major revision. The paper's most clinically important result is under-explained, and the fix costs nothing: state in Section 3.1 that a 42 percent first-degree share is clinically anomalous, state in Section 4.6 that the class prior on a clinically rare category is the likely driver of the 48/94 first-degree calls, and carry that into the Discussion in place of the current generic distribution-shift language. This also bears on the labels themselves — a community annotator calling erythema, healing burns and mild scalds all 'first degree' is a labelling-validity problem, not just a distribution-shift problem.
evidence: manuscript.tex line 154 (42 percent first degree) and line 192 (internal test 86 first degree of 205, i.e. 42 percent); line 235 states BIP_US gives 'a second-versus-third-degree probe with no first-degree cases'; line 464 reports 48 of 94 first-degree calls. external_validation_BIPUS.json confirms 48 of 94 rows have pred_pipeline == 'First' and contains no first-degree ground truth.

quote: Instrumented alternatives such as infrared thermography reach high accuracy but are expensive and rarely available \citep{dang}.
location: Section 1 (Introduction), manuscript.tex line 114
problem: Wrong exemplar. The instrumented reference standard for burn depth is laser Doppler imaging: it is the modality with regulatory clearance for this indication, it is validated against healing time at roughly 95 percent accuracy, and it is the one that is genuinely expensive and confined to specialist burn centres. Infrared thermography is the cheap end of the instrumented spectrum — smartphone-attachable IR modules cost a small fraction of an LDI unit — so citing it as the example of 'expensive and rarely available' inverts the actual cost structure a clinician recognises. LDI appears in the manuscript exactly once, buried in a limitations list at line 725 ('no thermography, no hyperspectral or laser-Doppler imaging'), and never in the Introduction where the clinical alternative to a photograph is set up.
why_it_matters: Minor revision, but it is the kind of slip that costs a paper credibility with a clinical referee in the first column. Name laser Doppler imaging as the instrumented comparator in the Introduction, state that it is validated against 3-week healing rather than against a degree label (which reinforces the taxonomy point in finding 1), and either drop 'expensive' from the thermography sentence or move it onto LDI where it belongs.
evidence: melba.bib entry {dang} is Dang et al., 'Use of infrared thermography for assessment of burn depth and healing potential: a systematic review', J Burn Care Res 2021 — a thermography review, which supports the accuracy clause but not the cost clause. grep over manuscript.tex: 'laser Doppler'/'Doppler' occurs only at line 725; the bibliography contains no laser-Doppler reference at all.

quote: The matched contrast, $2.07 \rightarrow 0.55$, is the smaller of the two and is the one we rely on; we give the 21-architecture figure because it is what the original experiment produced.
location: Section 3.2 (Source-grouped split and leakage control), manuscript.tex line 190; the same contrast carries the Abstract (line 100), Section 1 (line 124), Section 4.2 (line 270), Figure 2 caption (line 279), Table 11 row 1 (line 624), Section 5.1 (line 685) and the Conclusion (line 775).
problem: The 2.07 -> 0.55 contrast is matched on architectures but NOT on the number of training runs, and the paper's causal attribution of the whole 1.52 pp change to the split correction is therefore a non sequitur. The naive figure (+2.07) is one uncontrolled run per architecture; the leak-free figure (+0.55) is a mean over three seeds. Recomputing the leak-free side at a single run on the identical eight architectures gives +1.585 pp with 6 of 8 positive -- i.e. the same qualitative conclusion the leaky protocol gave (+2.07, 7 of 8 positive). The reversal from 'masking helps' to 'masking does not help' is delivered by seed averaging (seed 42 +1.59, seed 0 +0.24, seed 1 -0.18), which is a different one of the paper's own seven audited failure modes, not by the split correction. The paper itself identifies and eliminates exactly this class of confound elsewhere: 'Section 4.6 compared three seeds against ten, but those two protocols also differ in training recipe, so that comparison confounds seed count with the recipe change. The confound is avoidable' (line 514). No equivalent isolation is performed for the headline leakage contrast.
why_it_matters: This is the paper's title claim and its central novelty claim ('That combination, rather than any single ingredient, is what turned a null into a design recommendation', line 272). A referee who does the arithmetic finds that leakage removal alone does not turn the null; it moves +2.07 to +1.59. Major revision at minimum: the paper must report the run-matched contrast (2.07 -> 1.59) alongside the pooled one and rescope the causal claim, or a referee will conclude that the title claim is not established by the evidence presented. Note the broader thesis ('the evaluation protocol, not the architecture, determined the conclusion') survives intact -- it is only the leakage-specific attribution that fails, so the fix is a reframe, not new experiments.
evidence: /Volumes/RayTOSHIBA/مشروع تخرج ١/01_paper/statistics/benchmark1_masking_pooled_analysis.json, per_run field, restricted to seed 42 over the eight matched architectures (ConvNeXt-Large -2.93, DenseNet201 -0.98, EfficientNet-B0 +2.93, ResNet50 +0.98, SWIN-Base +4.39, SWIN-Small +2.44, SWIN-Tiny +2.93, ViT-Base +2.93): mean +1.585 pp, 6/8 positive. Seed 0 mean +0.244 (4/8), seed 1 mean -0.183 (3/8). /Volumes/RayTOSHIBA/مشروع تخرج ١/01_paper/statistics/benchmark0_LEAKY_21arch_naive_split.json gives one value per architecture with no seed field; /Volumes/RayTOSHIBA/مشروع تخرج ١/01_paper/statistics/DATA_LEAKAGE_FINDING.md line 37 records of the original code: 'No random seeds set.' The manuscript already knows the single-run leak-free value -- Figure 2's caption states 'the same comparison gives 1.51 percentage points at seed 42' -- but never pairs it with the single-run naive value.

quote: leakage here did not inflate a score, it changed the conclusion.
location: Abstract, manuscript.tex line 100; restated as the paper's single take-away in Section 6 (What we learned), line 751: 'leakage did not change our accuracy, it changed our conclusion.'
problem: The claim is factually false and is contradicted three lines away in the paper's own Results: 'where the masked accuracies were inflated by memorisation of near-duplicate training images' (Section 4.2, line 270). The leak did inflate a score -- the masked arm's -- and the authors have measured by how much. The dichotomy is also logically false: in a two-arm comparison, asymmetric score inflation IS score inflation; a leak that raises one arm's number necessarily moves the comparison. The defensible statement is 'the inflation was asymmetric, so it did not merely raise a number, it reversed the comparison', not 'it did not inflate a score'.
why_it_matters: A referee will read the bolded abstract sentence, then the authors' own text saying the accuracies were inflated, and conclude the paper's headline framing is self-contradictory and overstated -- damaging precisely because the paper's authority rests on scrupulous self-reporting. Major revision: reword the claim, and report the measured inflation (the paper currently reports no inflation magnitude at all for its own leak, which is a conspicuous omission in a paper about leakage magnitudes; grep for '13.7', '93.2', '82.2' in manuscript.tex returns nothing).
evidence: /Volumes/RayTOSHIBA/مشروع تخرج ١/01_paper/statistics/DATA_LEAKAGE_FINDING.md, 'Impact (measured on the real best_cnn_mask.pth)': masked Swin-Small scores 93.24% on the full 518-image naive test fold, 95.9% on the 417 leaked images, and 82.2% on the 101 leak-free images -- 'Leakage inflated this model by ~13.7 points.' The same file's clean-subset comparison (masked 82.2% against unmasked 88.81%) is a within-original-protocol, leakage-isolating measurement the manuscript never reports. benchmark0_LEAKY_21arch_naive_split.json confirms naive swin_small: unmasked 88.81, masked 93.05.

quote: What we have not found previously documented is the combination, an asymmetric split protocol that leaks into only one arm of a controlled comparison, with the per-arm leak rate measured on both sides.
location: Section 4.2 (Why the split matters), manuscript.tex line 272.
problem: The naive comparison was not a controlled comparison, by the paper's own account: 'The two arms of that original comparison therefore differed in split ratio and in test-set size as well as in leak rate' (Section 3.2, line 190) -- masked arm 70/15/15 with a 518-image test fold, unmasked arm 90/6/4 with a 143-image test fold, hence also different training-set sizes and entirely non-overlapping test images. The two arms are two separate experiments, not two conditions of one experiment. Calling this 'one arm of a controlled comparison' contradicts line 190, and it means the 2.07 -> 0.55 change is confounded with test-set identity, test-set size and training-set size in addition to leak rate. The paper asserts the extra differences make 'the confound larger... not smaller', but that is an assertion about how many things differ, not a demonstration that leakage is the operative cause. The paper knows the correct standard and applies it to a secondary result: 'That 12.7-point gap is not purely the leak, and we would be repeating this paper's own error if we reported it as though it were' (Section 4.11, line 601), followed by a 26-image control. No such control is run for the headline result, though one is available (re-split the unmasked arm at file level and re-run, or evaluate the naive masked model on its 101 leak-free test images).
why_it_matters: A referee can construct exactly the counter-reading the paper is trying to pre-empt: the leak inflated the masked model's score, the two arms were never on a common test set so no valid comparison existed to be 'changed', and the novelty claim ('what we have not found previously documented') therefore rests on a mischaracterisation of the original experiment. Major revision: either run the leakage-isolating control, or drop 'controlled comparison' and restate the finding as 'a protocol asymmetry, of which leakage was one component'.
evidence: manuscript.tex line 190 (split ratios, test-fold sizes, leak rates) versus line 272 ('controlled comparison'); /Volumes/RayTOSHIBA/مشروع تخرج ١/01_paper/statistics/DATA_LEAKAGE_FINDING.md table: CNN-DatasetM 2400/513/518 at 80.5% leak, CNN-DatasetNM 3081/200/143 at 0.0% leak. The same file's code audit records two further uncontrolled differences the manuscript never discloses for the naive arm: test-time augmentation applied to the test set, and hardcoded class weights '[100,50,30]' -- neither matches the corrected protocol described in Section 3.5 ('Training-time augmentation ... enabled and evaluation-time augmentation disabled', 'class-weighted cross-entropy using inverse class frequencies').

quote: Segmentation-guided classification therefore attains parity, not advantage, and it runs two models to do so.
location: Abstract, manuscript.tex line 98; repeated in Section 4.5 (line 382), Section 5 (line 679, 'The pipeline attains parity, not advantage') and Section 7 Conclusion (line 773).
problem: 'Parity' is an equivalence claim inferred from two non-significant tests (internal -0.29, p=0.65; external -1.79, p=0.11). This is absence of evidence read as evidence of absence, and the paper explicitly forbids that inference elsewhere: 'by the standard this paper applies elsewhere a non-significant result is not evidence of equivalence' (Table 6 note, line 425) and 'Overlapping error bars are not used as evidence of absence' (Section 3.6, line 231). No equivalence test against a pre-specified margin is performed. The external regime-B interval quoted at line 382 is -0.50 to +4.07, i.e. it is compatible with the plain classifier being 4 points better -- larger than any effect the paper claims to detect anywhere. The inconsistency is sharpened by the paper's own repeated position that the external comparison 'carries the paper's argument' (line 194) and 'is the result we rely on' (line 721): on that set the point estimate still favours the plain classifier in all three regimes (-1.47, -1.79, -2.57), and in regime C significantly so (p=0.008).
why_it_matters: The word 'parity' appears in the abstract, the discussion and the conclusion, and it is the paper's summary answer to its own research question. A referee applying the paper's own stated standard will require either a TOST/equivalence analysis against a stated margin, or a rewording to the claim the data support ('no configuration we tested outperformed the plain classifier; the difference is not resolved at ten seeds'). Major revision -- the fix is inferential wording plus one equivalence test, not new data.
evidence: manuscript.tex line 382 (p=0.65 internal, p=0.11 external, interval -0.50 to +4.07) against line 425 and line 231, which state the opposite inferential rule. Table 5 (tab:regimes, line 358-360) shows all three external paired differences negative, with regime C at -2.57, p=0.008. /Volumes/RayTOSHIBA/مشروع تخرج ١/01_paper/statistics/pipeline_regimes_10seed.json is the underlying ten-seed file.

quote: Nothing in our results suggests a route past parity, because the ceiling measured with perfect masks is already too low for one to exist.
location: Section 5.1 (Why segmentation did not win), manuscript.tex line 693; the same over-scoped bound appears in the Abstract (line 98, 'an upper bound on what any segmenter could contribute'), Section 5.1 (line 687, 'no improvement in segmentation could have rescued the design'), Section 5.4 (line 743) and Conclusion (line 773).
problem: The oracle ablation bounds one specific operator: hard multiplication by a human-drawn polygon, with the classifier trained and tested on that operator. It does not bound 'what any segmenter could contribute', because a segmenter emitting a differently shaped or softly weighted region is not dominated by the ground-truth polygon -- the paper's own mechanism section argues masking destroys useful global context, which implies a less aggressive region could beat the ground-truth mask. The existence claim in line 693 ('too low for one to exist') is a categorical non sequitur from a bounded ablation on a pooled mean. The paper contradicts it in its own Future Work: it proposes joint optimisation with 'the mask applied differentiably as a soft attention rather than a hard multiply' as 'Open, and in our view the most promising' (line 741) and ranks segmentation uncertainty 'alongside joint optimisation as the most direct test of whether the design can be rescued' (line 745). If the ceiling proved no route exists, there would be nothing left to test. Note the paper does correctly qualify the bound once, at line 213 ('That is a bound on the pooled mean across architectures, not on any single one'), but that qualifier is dropped everywhere the claim is actually used.
why_it_matters: This is the load-bearing argument for the paper's null ('it converts "our segmenter was not good enough" from an open excuse into a testable claim, and the test rejects it', line 687). A referee will note that the test rejects a narrower claim than the one stated, and that the paper's own future-work section concedes as much. Major revision: scope the bound explicitly to hard masking with annotator-drawn polygons pooled across architectures, and reconcile lines 687/693/743 with lines 741/745.
evidence: manuscript.tex line 213 (correct scoping: 'a bound on the pooled mean across architectures, not on any single one ... it therefore constrains, without excluding, the possibility that some untested masked configuration does better') versus lines 687, 693 and 773, which state the bound without the qualifier and as a categorical existence claim; lines 741 and 745 propose soft masking and joint optimisation as live routes to rescuing the design. The single dilation test that is offered as support (regime C, 12 px) is one point in a large operator space: Table 5 line 360 gives 83.27 internal against regime B's 83.32.

quote: Matching the training mask source to the test mask source recovers $+2.05$ of that ($p=0.041$), after which the two systems are statistically indistinguishable on both test sets ($-0.29$, $p=0.65$ internally; $-1.79$, $p=0.11$ externally, ten seeds each).
location: Abstract (l.98); Table 6 / Section 4.8 caption, l.350 ("Differences are paired by seed against the classifier."); compute disclosure Section 3.5, l.225
problem: The paper's central end-to-end conclusion — parity between pipeline and plain classifier — is a difference taken between two arms trained in separate campaigns, and Section 3.5 never says where the regime experiment ran. The regime pipeline accuracies (Table 6) come from a separate Kaggle kernel; the classifier they are differenced against is the ten-seed Colab head-to-head arm. Section 3.5 itself warns that Kaggle and Colab runs differ by "about two percentage points" and "are not [to be] mistaken for replicates of each other" — an offset larger than every difference in Table 6 (-2.34, +2.05, -0.29, -1.79). "Paired by seed" is also not pairing: a common seed index across two independent campaigns induces no correlation, so the paired t-test's variance reduction is unearned.
why_it_matters: Major revision at minimum, reject if it cannot be repaired. The abstract's claim "Segmentation-guided classification therefore attains parity, not advantage" is not established by a cross-environment difference whose magnitude is inside the environment offset the paper itself documents. A referee will require regimes A/B/C and the classifier baseline to be retrained in one environment under one recipe, or the parity claim withdrawn. The Section 3.5 compute paragraph must also be extended to cover the regime experiment, which it currently omits entirely.
evidence: /Volumes/RayTOSHIBA/مشروع تخرج ١/05_code/analysis/verify_paper_numbers.py l.640: "statistics/pipeline_regimes_10seed.json is a transcription of a Kaggle run." and l.644-645, log path code/kaggle-notebooks/logs/pipeline-10seed-regimes.stdout.log. The baseline hard-coded in statistics/pipeline_regimes_10seed.json ("internal": 83.61, "external": 77.81) equals the means of the classifier arm in statistics/h2h_10seed_paired.json (83.61 / 77.81, recomputed). Section 3.5 assigns "the head-to-head classifier retraining" to Colab A100 and Benchmark 1 to Kaggle P100, and names no environment for the regime runs. Magnitude check on the same platform gap: ConvNeXt-Large unmasked seed 42 is 84.88 on Kaggle (benchmark1_11arch_4cond_seed42.json) and 82.44 on Colab (benchmark2-proof/results/classifier_results.json), a 2.44 pp offset.

quote: Because every one of these subsets is drawn from the same ten runs under one recipe, this analysis carries no confound at all, and it isolates the seed count as the cause.
location: Section 4.10 ("The range of answers any three of these ten seeds would give"), l.514
problem: The ten runs are not under one recipe, by the paper's own statement three pages earlier. Table 8's footnote (l.425) says "Seeds 0--6 used batch 16 at learning rate $10^{-4}$ and seeds 7--9 batch 32 at $2\times10^{-4}$, a change made for compute reasons." The 120 three-seed subsets are therefore a mixture: 35 draw only from recipe 1, exactly 1 draws only from recipe 2, and 84 straddle both. The subset spread that the paper attributes wholly to seed count is partly recipe variance — the very confound the same paragraph claims to have removed from the three-vs-ten comparison. The claim "it isolates the seed count as the cause" is false as written.
why_it_matters: Major revision. This is a headline claim: it appears in the abstract ("of the 120 three-seed subsets of ten runs, only 15 detect it"), in Section 4.10, and in Section 5 ("Of the 120 three-seed subsets of our ten runs, only 15 detect the external effect"). A referee reviewing a paper whose thesis is protocol rigour will not accept a self-contradicted no-confound claim. The fix is available and cheap: re-run the subset analysis restricted to the 35 within-recipe subsets of seeds 0-6, report that number, and delete the "no confound at all" sentence.
evidence: Manuscript l.425 (Table 8 footnote) states the two recipes explicitly. Confirmed in the raw data: statistics/h2h_10seed_paired.json carries a per-run "recipe" field reading "batch16_lr1e-4" for seeds 0-6 and "batch32_lr2e-4" for seeds 7-9, for both arms. C(7,3)=35 subsets are recipe-pure for group 1, C(3,3)=1 for group 2, leaving 84 mixed.

quote: As built, with its classifier trained on ground-truth masks and tested on predicted ones, it trails the plain classifier by 2.34 points internally ($p=0.025$).
location: Abstract (l.98), against Section 4.6 (l.394) and Section 4.11 (l.605); Table 6 caption (l.350)
problem: The paper reports three mutually inconsistent ten-seed internal margins for what it describes as one and the same system. Abstract/Table 6: -2.34, p=0.025 (pipeline mean 81.27). Section 4.6/Table 8: +2.63, p=0.032 (pipeline mean 80.98). Section 4.11: +2.73, p=0.016 (pipeline mean 80.88). All three are ten seeds, all three are the ground-truth-trained, predicted-mask-tested Swin-Tiny pipeline, all three are differenced against the same 83.61 classifier. Table 6's caption asserts "Regime A is the published configuration," but regime A is a different set of training runs from the head-to-head pipeline arm (per-seed values diverge by up to 4.4 pp, e.g. seed 6: 84.39 vs 80.00). The manuscript never reconciles the three, and the abstract quotes the smallest — the one most favourable to the pipeline.
why_it_matters: Major revision. A referee will ask which number is the paper's estimate of the as-built internal margin, and will note that a paper built on disclosing its own evaluation slips has quietly selected the most flattering of three values for its abstract. The paper must state that regime A is a re-run rather than the published configuration, give one designated estimate, and show the other two as replication spread.
evidence: statistics/pipeline_regimes_10seed.json regime A internal mean 81.268 (per-seed 82.44, 83.41, 80.49, 83.90, 82.44, 81.46, 80.00, 80.00, 80.00, 78.54); statistics/h2h_10seed_paired.json pipeline arm mean 80.98 (per-seed 82.93, 80.49, 79.02, 81.95, 77.56, 81.46, 84.39, 79.02, 83.41, 79.51); benchmark2-proof/results/pipeline_arm_leakfree_raw.json mean 80.88. The authors' own file statistics/pipeline_best_chance.json holds "published_pipeline_10seed": 80.88 as a field distinct from its arm A, i.e. the raw data already treat regime A and the published pipeline as different runs.

quote: Swin-Tiny on ground-truth (oracle) masks reached 83.9 percent internally, an upper bound; the robust pipeline with real predicted masks reached 81.5 percent at the same seed and 78.9 $\pm$ 1.0 percent across seeds, so at matched seeds imperfect segmentation costs about two points.
location: Section 4.9 (l.458) and Table 4 oracle row (l.327), against Abstract (l.98) and Section 5 (l.679); upper-bound argument at Section 5.1 (l.687)

location: Table 5 (Section 4.5, "Giving the pipeline its best configuration"), manuscript.tex line 358; contradicted by Section 4.6 line 394 and Table 6 line 415

why_it_matters: Return before review. A referee who tabulates the paper's own end-to-end result gets 2.34, 2.63 and 2.73 for the internal margin and 1.47 versus 2.79 (p=0.085 versus p=0.005) for the external margin, and cannot tell which the paper stands behind. For a manuscript whose entire claim to authority is that every number is recomputable and whose thesis is that unstable numbers mislead, an unreconciled duplicate of the headline experiment is the single thing most likely to sink it in review. The fix is cheap (state that Table 5 is a separate ten-seed retraining under a uniform recipe, give its recipe, and say which estimate the abstract quotes and why) but it must be made before referees see it.

quote: The two arms of that original comparison therefore differed in split ratio and in test-set size as well as in leak rate, which we state because it makes the confound larger than a single-split description would suggest, not smaller.
location: Section 3.2 ("Source-grouped split and leakage control"), manuscript.tex line 190
problem: The title, abstract, Section 4.2, Section 6 and the Conclusion all attribute the 2.07 -> 0.55 change in the masking effect to leakage specifically ("leakage here did not inflate a score, it changed the conclusion"; "Leakage therefore did not inflate a number but manufactured a comparative conclusion"). But by the authors' own sentence above, the naive-split comparison differed from the corrected one in at least four ways at once: leak rate (80.5% vs 0%), split ratio (a 70/15/15 re-split vs the collection's own 90/6/4), test-fold size and identity (518 vs 143 images in the original arms; 205 in the corrected one), and, for the 3.06 figure, architecture pool (21 vs 11/8). No experiment isolates leakage from the other three. A leak-free file-level re-split at the same 70/15/15 ratio would have identified it and was not run. The paper holds itself to exactly this standard elsewhere and refuses the parallel inference: "That 12.7-point gap is not purely the leak, and we would be repeating this paper's own error if we reported it as though it were" (Section 4.11, line 601), where it declines to attribute a 12.7 pp drop to leakage because a 21% training-set reduction is confounded with it. The title claim is granted the attribution that the segmentation result is denied.
why_it_matters: Major revision. The methodological novelty the paper claims — "an asymmetric split protocol that leaks into only one arm of a controlled comparison, with the per-arm leak rate measured on both sides" — rests entirely on this causal attribution, and a referee who reads line 190 will say the mechanism is plausible but not identified. Either run the ratio-matched leaky control, or restate the claim as "an asymmetrically prepared comparison, of which differential leakage is the dominant suspected cause", and soften the title accordingly.
evidence: Manuscript line 190 (arms differ in split ratio, test-set size and leak rate); line 601 (the paper's own refusal to make the same attribution for the 12.7 pp segmentation gap, and its statement that "a properly powered separation would need the leak-free model retrained at the original training-set size"); line 272 ("Leakage therefore did not inflate a number but manufactured a comparative conclusion"); title, line 76. The 2.07 figure derives from 8 architectures on the naive split (statistics/benchmark0_LEAKY_21arch_naive_split.json) and 0.55 from 24 architecture-seed pairs on the corrected split (statistics/benchmark1_masking_pooled_analysis.json) — different pools as well as different splits.

quote: After also dropping the fourth-degree class and remapping the remainder to first, second, and third degree, 319 images remain, distributed 139, 157, and 23, drawn from \textbf{175 distinct source photographs} (mean 1.8 images per source, maximum 4).
location: Section 3.6 ("Evaluation protocol and statistics"), manuscript.tex line 235; summarised in Table 1
problem: The construction of the clean external set does not add up as described, and 934 images are unaccounted for. The paragraph states the collection "contained 1{,}371 images from 199 source photographs" and that the perceptual-hash check "removed 118 images", leaving 1,253. The only further step described is dropping the fourth-degree class, after which 319 remain — which would require 934 of 1,253 images (75%) to be fourth-degree burns, an implausible class distribution for any burn collection. The per-source counts confirm an undescribed step: the source collection averages 6.9 images per source (1,371/199) while the retained set averages 1.8 with a maximum of 4, so copies were dropped per source by some rule the manuscript never states. As written, the described procedure cannot produce 319 images from 1,371, and a referee will read the gap either as an arithmetic error or as an undisclosed selection step applied to the paper's most load-bearing evaluation set. One or two sentences naming the missing step (and its class-wise effect) fixes it.

quote: Split-after-augmentation leakage is itself documented \citep{yagis2021,tampu2022}.
location: Section 4.2 "Why the split matters: an augmentation-induced leakage artifact" (manuscript.tex line 272); the same conflation appears in Section 2 at line 146
problem: Neither cited work studies splitting after augmentation. Yagis et al. 2021 studies splitting 3D MRI volumes at the 2D slice level rather than the subject level; Tampu et al. 2022 studies splitting 2D images taken from OCT volumes, where "consecutive images are often very similar in both visible structures and noise." Both are within-volume near-duplicate leakage; neither involves augmented copies of a source image. Section 2 compounds this by introducing them as instances of the augmentation mechanism: "A concrete and easily reproduced form of leakage in image work is splitting after augmentation, so that augmented copies of one source image land in both folds. Quantified case studies of this kind exist" — followed immediately by the two slice-level examples.
why_it_matters: Major revision. The sentence sits inside the paper's novelty-scoping argument: "Split-after-augmentation leakage is itself documented [...] What we have not found previously documented is the combination, an asymmetric split protocol that leaks into only one arm of a controlled comparison." A referee who knows this literature will see that the claimed prior documentation of the first ingredient does not exist in the cited papers, which undermines the credibility of the scoping claim in a paper whose selling point is precision about leakage mechanisms — and whose own leakage is genuinely augmentation-driven ("about 2.5 copies per source"), so the distinction is not cosmetic.
evidence: Yagis 2021 abstract (Sci Rep 11:22544): "we quantitatively assessed the effect of a data leakage caused by 3D MRI data splitting based on a 2D slice-level". Tampu 2022 abstract (Sci Data 9:580): "it is common to train classification networks using 2D images originating from volumetric data [...] an inappropriate data split can result in overlap between the training and testing sets". Neither abstract nor either title mentions augmentation. The manuscript itself describes the mechanisms correctly two sentences earlier ("Splitting brain MRI at the slice rather than the subject level"), which makes the line-272 assertion internally inconsistent as well.

quote: It judges six of fourteen studies to carry a high risk of bias, faults the reliance on public datasets that do not represent the target population, and reports dataset details as frequently unstated \citep{fu2026review}.

The claim is used to set up the paper's own contribution on data hygiene, and a referee who opens the review will find that the manuscript has attributed to it a finding it does not contain. quote: Leakage has recently been shown to inflate prediction performance across a range of mechanisms in neuroimaging \citep{rosenblatt2024}
location: Section 1 Introduction (manuscript.tex line 116)
problem: Rosenblatt et al. found the opposite of "across a range of mechanisms": of the five forms of leakage they tested, only two inflated performance, and the others did not. Their abstract states "Leakage via feature selection and repeated subjects drastically inflates prediction performance, whereas other forms of leakage have minor effects", and their results section reports leaky covariate regression actively *decreasing* performance. The manuscript's own Related work characterises the same paper correctly and in direct contradiction to the Introduction: "The picture is not uniform: in connectome-based prediction, some forms of leakage inflate performance substantially while others have minor or even negative effects \citep{rosenblatt2024}."
why_it_matters: Minor revision. On its own it is a loose sentence, but this paper's entire claim to authority is that it characterises leakage more carefully than the literature does, and it contradicts itself about a leakage paper across twenty pages. A reviewer noticing the internal inconsistency will read the rest of the citations less charitably.

quote: it has been applied to burns for two coupled subproblems, segmenting the burn region and classifying its severity \citep{boissin}
location: Section 1 Introduction (manuscript.tex line 116); repeated at Section 2 line 138 as "delineating the burn region and grading its severity \citep{boissin}"
problem: Boissin et al. do not classify severity. Their two algorithms "respectively identify burns, and classify whether they require surgery" — a binary surgical-need decision, not a depth or degree grade. Separately, and more consequentially, Boissin is the one burn-specific paper in this bibliography that stratifies performance by Fitzpatrick skin type, and reports a directionally split result ("The wound identifier algorithm was more accurate in patients with darker skin types; the wound classifier was more accurate in patients with lighter skin types"). Sections 3.7, 4.9 and 5.4 discuss skin tone at length and conclude "Whether these models are equitable across skin tones remains genuinely unknown" without citing it.
why_it_matters: Minor revision. The severity/surgery slip is a one-word fix. The omission is the substantive half: a referee will ask why an entire section on skin-tone dependence, plus a limitation paragraph asserting the question is unanswered, ignores a prior burn study in the paper's own reference list that reports skin-type-stratified accuracy — especially since Boissin's split direction is exactly the kind of non-replicating pattern this paper argues for reporting.

An additional aim assessed the performances in different Fitzpatrick skin types. [...] The wound identifier algorithm was more accurate in patients with darker skin types; the wound classifier was more accurate in patients with lighter skin types." grep of manuscript.tex shows \citep{boissin} appears only at lines 116 and 138, both in the two-subproblem framing.
